title: Historical Map Context: Anchor Old Maps to Today
description: Use Historical Map Context to read old maps against precise modern coordinates and outlines — where that vanished street or border sits today. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a great-grandfather's 1910 street name no longer exists — but its junction's modern coordinates place the house within a few doors of a current address.
quick_answer: Historical Map Context helps you read old maps against the modern world: pin the places an old map names to precise modern latitude and longitude, and use clean modern outlines to orient yourself. It is an anchor for historical reading — honest orientation, not warped-image georeferencing.
steps_intro: Old maps speak a dead geography — here is how to translate it into today's:

A mill on an 1840 tithe map, a railway that closed in 1963 — anchor each to today's streets and the archive becomes walkable.
Students compare an old county map with the modern outline and list what changed: borders, names, a drained lake. The

Old field names and plot lines raise questions modern coordinates can frame properly — while remembering that legal answers belong to surveyors and archives, not web maps.
A 1905 directory lists a shop on a street renamed twice since. Its junction with a surviving cross-street gives a modern coordinate pair; the shop's block is identifiable today within a few doors.

A village recorded in one country in 1900 and another by 1950 never moved — the border did. Modern coordinates separate the place's fixed position from the century's politics, the core skill this page supports.

faq: Can I upload a scan of my old map?

Not here — this is a context and anchoring tool, not an image-upload georeferencer. Scanned-map warping belongs in GIS software (QGIS's georeferencer is the free standard) with this page's coordinates as your control-point reference.

Wildly variable. A 19th-century Ordnance Survey sheet can be accurate to metres; a 17th-century county map may misplace towns by kilometres. Treat every old map's geometry as a claim to test against modern anchors.
Why is the longitude on my old map 'wrong'?
It may be measured from a different prime meridian — Paris, Ferro, or a national observatory. Convert by the known offset (Paris is 2.337°E of Greenwich) before concluding the mapmaker erred.
Where do I find old maps to work with?

National library digital collections (the British Library, Library of Congress, Gallica), national mapping agencies' archives and university map libraries all publish scans freely. Their catalogues are the researcher's real starting point.
Can modern coordinates settle a boundary dispute from an old map?
No. They can show where features sit today; title and boundary law run on deeds, surveys and courts. Use this page for understanding, professionals for verdicts.
What is a tithe map or enclosure map?

British parish maps made for tax (tithe) and land-reorganisation (enclosure) purposes in the 18th–19th centuries — extraordinarily detailed for fields and owners, and the genealogist's favourite anchor documents.
Do place names on old maps use different spellings?
Constantly — standardised spelling is recent. Search archives with variant spellings and the parish or district name; the coordinates you anchor will outlast the orthography debate.
Can I print a then-and-now pair?
Yes: capture the modern outline or map view with Map PNG Export at the same framing as your old map excerpt and print them side by side — the honest comparison format this page encourages.
